text: Users self-register as either Client or Freelancer. Arbitrator, Auditor and Administrator accounts can only be created by an Administrator.
Registration requires full name, unique email, password, role choice and acceptance of a clear “simulation only – no real money” notice.
Email ownership is verified through a single-use link that expires after 24 hours; unverified accounts cannot log in.
Passwords must be at least 12 characters and are rejected if found in a list of common or breached passwords.
Passwords are stored only as Argon2id (or bcrypt, cost 12+) hashes and are never written to logs or responses.
Login errors are generic (“invalid email or password”) so attackers cannot discover which emails are registered.
After 5 consecutive failed logins the account is locked for 15 minutes and further attempts are rate-limited per IP and per account.

TOTP multi-factor authentication is optional for Clients and Freelancers, mandatory for Arbitrators, Auditors and Administrators, and required for any release, refund or withdrawal above the configured threshold (default 50,000 SC).
Access tokens expire after 15 minutes; refresh tokens rotate on every use, last at most 7 days, and are revoked on logout or password change.
Sessions time out after 30 minutes of inactivity.
Password reset uses a single-use token that expires after 15 minutes; all active sessions are revoked after a reset.
Role-based access control (Client, Freelancer, Arbitrator, Auditor, Administrator) is enforced on the server for every endpoint; hiding a button in the UI is never treated as authorization.
Users can update display name and notification preferences but can never change their own role.
Every user has a simulated wallet holding an Available balance and a Held (escrowed) balance in Simulation Credits (SC), stored as integer minor units (no floating point).
Clients can top up their wallet through the Simulated Payment Gateway (minimum 10 SC, maximum 100,000 SC per top-up, 500,000 SC per day).
The system never collects or stores real card, bank or mobile-money credentials; the top-up form uses simulated instruments only.
Freelancers can withdraw Available balance to a simulated bank or mobile-money destination; each withdrawal is logged.
All money movements are recorded in a double-entry ledger: every transaction has balanced debit and credit entries, so the sum of all ledger entries is always zero.
Wallet balances can never go negative; any operation that would cause an overdraft is rejected with no partial effect.
Every money-moving request carries an idempotency key; a repeated request with the same key returns the original result and moves no additional funds.
Users can view and filter transaction history (date, type, contract) and export it to CSV or PDF.
The Simulated Payment Gateway can be configured (in test/demo mode) to return success, failure, timeout or a delayed callback so error paths can be tested.
A Client creates a contract with title, description, freelancer (by email or username), total amount in SC, deadline, review period (default 3 days) and revision limit (default 2).
A contract has at least one milestone; optionally up to 10 milestones, each with its own amount, deliverable description and due date. Milestone amounts must add up to the contract total.
The Freelancer can accept, reject (with reason) or counter-propose. A counter- proposal creates a new contract version that the Client must accept.
Contract terms become immutable once funded. Later amendments require approval from both parties and are stored as a new version.
Every contract has a unique ID and changes state only through the escrow state machine defined in Section 7.
Illegal state transitions (for example releasing an unfunded contract) are rejected with a clear error and recorded in the audit log.
Before funding, either party may cancel without penalty. After funding, cancellation needs mutual consent or must go through a dispute.
Proposals not answered within 7 days (configurable) automatically expire.
Both parties see a contract timeline showing every event with a UTC timestamp and the acting user.

A user can only see contracts they are a party to. An Arbitrator can only see contracts of disputes assigned to them; an Auditor has read-only access; an Administrator sees metadata but not deliverable contents.
Contracts can be searched and filtered by status, date range and counterparty.
All free-text contract fields are length-limited, validated and output-encoded to prevent injection and XSS.
A Client can fund an Accepted contract from their Available balance; the amount moves to Held balance in one atomic transaction.
Funding is rejected if the balance is insufficient, the contract is not in the Accepted state, or the amount does not match the contract total.
On successful funding the contract moves to Funded and the Freelancer is notified to start work.
Held funds cannot be spent, withdrawn or transferred by either party; they only move through release, refund or dispute resolution.
Funding uses database transactions with row-level locking (or optimistic version checks) so two simultaneous requests can never fund the same contract twice.
The platform fee (default 2% of the contract value, configurable by an Administrator) is shown to both parties before acceptance and deducted at release.
Accepted contracts that are not funded within 7 days automatically expire.
The Freelancer marks a milestone as Delivered by uploading a deliverable (allow- listed types: zip, pdf, png, jpg, docx, txt; maximum 25 MB) with an optional note.
Uploaded files are stored encrypted, validated by content type as well as file extension, and their SHA-256 hash is recorded at upload and shown to both parties.
Delivery starts the review period (default 3 days) with a visible countdown.
During the review period the Client can approve, request a revision (with reason) or raise a dispute.
Funds are released only when BOTH parties have confirmed: the Freelancer’s delivery confirmation and the Client’s approval (or automatic approval when the review period expires).
A revision request returns the contract to In Progress and increments the revision counter. Once the limit is reached, the Client can only approve or dispute.
If the Client takes no action, the scheduler auto-approves when the review period ends, after a reminder 24 hours before.
Release calculates the fee, debits Held, credits the Freelancer and the fee account, and writes ledger and audit entries in a single atomic transaction.
Release is idempotent: repeated or concurrent release requests can never pay out twice.
Both parties receive a receipt (in-app and simulated email) for every release, refund or split.
Deliverables are downloaded only by the two parties (and the assigned Arbitrator during a dispute) through short-lived signed links.
Either party may raise a dispute while the contract is Funded, In Progress or Delivered, choosing a reason category and giving a description.
Raising a dispute freezes the Held funds: release, refund and withdrawal are blocked until the dispute is resolved.
Both parties can submit evidence (text and up to 5 files each) during an evidence window (default 5 days). Evidence is hashed and cannot be edited or deleted after submission.
An Administrator assigns an Arbitrator who is not a party to the contract (automatic assignment is also supported).
The Arbitrator can view the contract, timeline, deliverables and both parties’ evidence, and can request additional information from either party.
The Arbitrator decides one of: Release to Freelancer, Refund to Client, or Split (percentage), and must record a written rationale.
The decision executes the matching ledger movements atomically, moves the contract to a terminal state, and notifies both parties.
Both parties can withdraw a dispute by mutual consent, returning the contract to its previous state.
Arbitrators must decide within 7 days (configurable); overdue disputes escalate to an Administrator.
An Arbitrator with a relationship to either party (same contract history) is blocked from assignment.
A single appeal to a second Arbitrator is possible within 48 hours of a decision.
An in-app notification is created for every contract state change that affects a user.
Simulated email notifications (captured by a development mail catcher) are sent for: invitation, funding, delivery, revision request, approval, release, dispute, resolution and security alerts.

Users can choose which non-critical notifications they receive per channel.
Notifications never contain sensitive content such as passwords, tokens or
Notification delivery status is tracked (queued, sent, failed).

Secrets (passwords, tokens, file contents) are never written to the audit log.

Suspended users cannot log in or trigger transitions; their funded contracts are frozen and flagged for review.
A reconciliation report proves that wallets + Held + fee account = total credits issued (ledger invariant).
Administrators can never edit or delete ledger or audit records; corrections are made with compensating entries.
Client and Freelancer dashboards show active contracts, Held funds, completed contracts and open disputes.
Users can export statements and contract summaries to PDF or CSV.
Administrators can export a simulation summary (volumes, dispute rate, average time-to-release).
Dashboards refresh at least every 30 seconds.
The interface supports English, with Swahili as an optional second language.
All traffic uses TLS 1.2+ (HTTPS only, HSTS enabled).
Deliverables and sensitive fields are encrypted at rest with AES-256; keys are held outside the codebase.
All inputs are validated on the server with allow-lists; database access uses parameterized queries or an ORM only (no string-built SQL).
All output is context-encoded and a strict Content-Security-Policy is set; cookies are HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite.
State-changing requests are protected against CSRF; authorization is checked per object to prevent IDOR (a user cannot fetch another user’s contract by changing an ID).
API rate limiting: 100 requests per minute per user and stricter limits on login, reset and money-moving endpoints.
Secrets (JWT keys, DB passwords) are supplied through environment variables or a secret manager and are never committed to Git; secret scanning runs in CI.
Dependencies are scanned for known vulnerabilities on every build and critical findings block the merge.
The system is designed against the OWASP Top 10 and verified against selected OWASP ASVS Level 2 controls.
Money is represented as integers; rounding rules are defined once and unit-tested.
Every multi-step financial operation is atomic (all-or-nothing) with rollback on failure.
The ledger invariant (sum of all entries = 0, no negative balances) is checked automatically after every test run and by the reconciliation job.
Concurrent requests on the same contract are serialized (locking or version checks) so no double funding, double release or lost update is possible.
Time-based rules (auto-approve, expiry) use server UTC time only; client clocks are never trusted.
95% of API requests respond in under 500 ms under a load of 200 concurrent users.
Pages load within 2 seconds on a typical 4G connection.
A release or refund completes within 2 seconds including ledger and audit writes.
Audit chain verification handles 100,000 entries within 60 seconds.
Target availability of 99% during the demo/assessment period.
Database backups run at least daily and a restore has been tested at least once.
The scheduler is restart-safe: jobs missed during downtime run on recovery and each job is idempotent.
Health-check endpoints exist for the API, database and scheduler.
A new Client can create and fund a contract within 5 minutes without training.
Every screen makes the escrow state, held amount and next required action obvious.
The interface is responsive from 320 px to 1920 px and aims at WCAG 2.1 AA (contrast 4.5:1, keyboard navigation, labelled inputs).
Destructive or irreversible actions (release, refund, dispute) require an explicit confirmation step summarising the consequence.
Error messages are specific and tell the user what to do next.
The codebase follows SOLID principles with separate modules for authentication, contracts, ledger, escrow state machine, disputes, audit and notifications (see Section 11).
Automated unit-test coverage of at least 80% overall and 95% for the ledger, state machine and audit modules.
Every push triggers the CI pipeline (lint, unit tests, integration tests, dependency and static- analysis scans); merges to main require a passing pipeline and one code review.
All work is tracked as Jira issues linked to commits and pull requests.
The external payment dependency is behind an interface so the simulated gateway can be replaced without changing business logic.
Only the minimum personal data is collected (name, email, role); no real financial credentials are ever collected.

Data-handling follows the principles of the Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 and GDPR (purpose limitation, minimization, right to access and erasure by anonymization where financial history must be kept).
Audit and ledger records are designed to be retained for a long period (assumed 7 years, as in real financial systems) even though this is a simulation.
A visible notice on every money screen states that no real money is used.
